analysis.problem_symptom: Gaming PC will not power on via the front power button after being shut down. It only powers on after performing a 'hard power reset' by cycling the power supply switch off, holding the power button for 10 seconds (to drain flea power), and then cycling the power supply back on. Additionally, the GPU was running at 1/4 of its intended speed due to incorrect slot placement.
analysis.hardware_specs: Motherboard (Asus, with BIOS Flashback feature), GPU (NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2060), Power Supply Unit (PSU).
diagnostic_steps: Observed the primary symptom: PC fails to power on normally, requiring flea power drain.
Hypothesized the issue could be related to flea power, motherboard power management, or PSU.
Tested the Power Supply Unit (PSU) using a 'Doctor power 3 power supply tester'; PSU tested fine and could be cycled on/off continuously without issue, ruling out PSU failure.
Concluded the problem was on the motherboard side.
Observed a blinking LED light on the motherboard, identified as the indicator for the BIOS Flashback button.
Recalled known issues with certain Asus motherboards where the BIOS Flashback feature can get stuck in a loop, preventing normal power-on (a security prevention feature).
Identified a secondary issue: The GPU (2060) was installed in a secondary PCIe slot, which was only a x4 connection, significantly bottlenecking its performance compared to the primary x16 slot.
analysis.root_cause: The primary root cause was a faulty or stuck BIOS Flashback feature on the Asus motherboard. This caused the system to constantly attempt to flash the BIOS, preventing the power button from initiating startup. The secondary root cause was the GPU being incorrectly installed in a PCIe x4 slot instead of the primary PCIe x16 slot.
solution: For the BIOS Flashback issue (temporary fix): Accessed the BIOS (Advanced Mode -> Advanced -> APM Configuration) and enabled 'Energy Related Products Ready' (ERP Ready) to 'S4+S5'. This restricts power to extra features like the BIOS Flashback button in S4/S5 shutdown states, preventing it from activating automatically.
For the BIOS Flashback issue (recommended permanent fix): Advised the customer to RMA the motherboard.
For the GPU bottleneck: Moved the GPU from the secondary PCIe x4 slot to the primary PCIe x16 slot to ensure full bandwidth communication with the CPU.
analysis.key_tech_takeaway: When a PC fails to power on and requires a 'flea power' drain (PSU switch off, hold power button) to start, investigate motherboard power management or specific features like BIOS Flashback. A blinking BIOS Flashback LED on Asus motherboards can indicate a stuck or looping feature preventing startup; temporarily disabling 'ERP Ready (S4+S5)' in BIOS can mitigate this, but RMA is often the permanent fix. Always ensure GPUs are installed in the primary PCIe x16 slot for optimal performance, as secondary slots may have fewer lanes (e.g., x4) and create a significant bottleneck.

transcript: This gaming PC has one of the worst all in one liquid coolers you could have. Not because it's a 240 millimeter size, nor because of the brand, but rather because of the style and design that causes these coolers to fail more than just about any other on the market. All because they were trying to avoid paying usage rights for a patent cut cost, obviously. Because if you look at just about any other AIO, they use what's called a pump block combo. Which is exactly what it sounds like. Where the water block that sits on your CPU also has the pump inside to move the hot fluid away from your CPU to be cooled off by your radiator and then pump it back through cold back over to the water block itself. You go ahead and continue the cycle over and over again, and for the most part that's how you'll see most AIOs work. Except for this one, because the manufacturer, that's not even I by power, that's just a logo, decide to move the pump from the water block to the radiator. And they did this because this design is actually patented by a company called Acetek, who makes the vast majority of AIOs today, especially the pump block combos for most brands out there. But as some coolers are so cheap that they can't afford to pay the royalty to Asus Tech, they come up with solutions like this by putting the pump In the radiator to bypass the patent to save cost at the expense of the customer, as these AIOs are terrible because one, by having the pump up here, this little square area blocks off surface area that you could be using to keep your CPU cool, hurting performance in the process. But what's even worse is that although every AI deals with some level of evaporation that lets air inside of your loop, when you actually mount these radiators on the top of your case, what happens is you have your pump at the highest point of your loop, right where those air bubbles are gonna gather, which results in air getting inside your pump, making it incredibly noisy and often resulting in premature failure. If you do happen to own one of these terrible AIs, a couple things that you can do to save your pump, if it hasn't failed already, is to actually rotate where your radiator is mounted. analysis.problem_symptom: Poor CPU cooling performance, excessive pump noise, and premature failure of the All-In-One (AIO) liquid cooler.
analysis.hardware_specs: Gaming PC, 240mm AIO liquid cooler (often found in systems from brands like iBuyPower), CPU, radiator, water block, pump, PC case.
diagnostic_steps: Observation of AIO cooler design, specifically identifying the pump integrated into the radiator rather than the CPU water block.
Analysis of the design's inherent flaws leading to common failure modes, including reduced cooling surface area and air accumulation in the pump when mounted at the top of the case.
analysis.root_cause: The AIO liquid cooler's design, where the pump is integrated into the radiator instead of the CPU water block. This design choice, often made to bypass patent royalties (e.g., Acetek's pump-block combo patent), leads to two main issues: 1) The pump's location on the radiator reduces effective cooling surface area, hurting performance. 2) When mounted at the top of a PC case, the radiator-integrated pump becomes the highest point in the loop, causing air bubbles to gather in the pump, leading to noise and premature failure due to cavitation and lack of fluid.
analysis.solution: For existing problematic AIOs: Re-mount the radiator to the front of the PC case to ensure the pump is no longer the highest point in the loop, preventing air accumulation. Otherwise, replace the faulty AIO cooler with a more reliable pump-block combo AIO or an air cooler.
analysis.key_tech_takeaway: Avoid AIO liquid coolers where the pump is integrated into the radiator, as this design is prone to premature failure and poor performance, especially when mounted at the top of a PC case. If such a cooler must be used, always mount the radiator on the front of the case to keep the pump below the highest point of the loop, mitigating air bubble issues. Opt for AIOs with a pump-block combo design (e.g., Acetek-patented designs) for better reliability and performance.

Regardless, just as the name implies, these modern GPUs have the ability to cut off their fans completely as long as the GPU temperature is under a certain threshold. Often when your system's idling, doing any task that's not GPU intensive, where it's not going to produce Enough heat that the built in heat sink can't passively dissipate using the airflow from the rest of the case without having to kick on these fans. analysis.problem_symptom: GPU fans are not spinning while the PC is powered on and idling.
analysis.hardware_specs: Modern dedicated graphics card (GPU) with axial cooling fans and integrated heatsink
diagnostic_steps: Observed GPU fans stationary during idle and low-load desktop operation.
Analyzed GPU thermal behavior, passive heatsink dissipation, and firmware fan curve profiles.
analysis.root_cause: Normal operation of the GPU manufacturer's Zero RPM / 0dB mode, which keeps fans stopped until a specific temperature threshold is reached.
analysis.solution: Educated customer that no hardware repair is needed; confirmed fans automatically engage once GPU load and core temperatures increase past the thermal threshold.
analysis.key_tech_takeaway: Stationary GPU fans during low-load tasks or desktop idle indicate active Zero RPM mode designed to reduce noise and fan bearing wear; fans should only be suspected of failure if they remain stopped when temperatures exceed operating thresholds (typically 55-60°C).

title: Intel Evo Vs Intel VPro #tech #techtok #pcrepair #computerrepair #lap...
transcript: What's the difference between Intel EVO and Intel vpro? Well, they're both certification platforms put on by Intel, but the main difference is one's for consumers and one's for businesses. The Intel EVO program is basically the premium Ultrabook lineup of laptops with Intel CPUs. They have to have great battery life, they have to be portable, great connectivity, and a bunch of other minor requirements. On the other hand, Intel vpro is all about the management and security side of a laptop, making it easier for IT administration. One of the main security differences for Intel V Pro is the fact that it has to have on board security that goes beyond the actual operating system level. This means that IT administrators can manage that security and set up certain profiles to protect from additional threats that you may not normally see on the consumer side that would target something like the BIOS or other aspects of the back into the computer that could open the system up for a vulnerability. And then the other thing that's huge for IT departments is the active management that has to be built in. Basically, on a traditional like, management platform, you can have a laptop be managed with a tool, but it doesn't do anything on the back end of the computer, or if the operating system is not working, or if you happen to have a laptop that's off, there's nothing you can do. But with the Intel vpro system, You can actually turn on a computer remotely as well as access it from a remote location, even when it's not working properly. It makes the lives of a system administrator a lot easier, and it's something that is vital in business environments. You may have in points deployed all over the world. And that's why there's a massive premium if you end up buying an Intel vpro laptop. But for most consumers, those features really don't matter. So if you do want a certification platform to make sure you're getting the best ultrabooks, look at the Intel EVO program. And you can kind of forget about vpro unless you're a system administrator.

title: UBREAKIFIX Screwed Our Customer! #tech #techtok #pcrepair #computerre...

title: Don’t Mix and Match Power Supply Cables! #tech #techtok #pcrepair #co...
transcript: When changing something out like a power supply, the cables you use really matter. And even if the cables happen to fit between multiple power supplies, don't ever use them. Example of what I mean by this is this PC right here that just came into my shop. See, it was actually taken to another repair shop before coming here because the system was crashing in games and that other shop determined that it was a lack of power. So they went ahead and changed up the power supply to a pretty strong 1000 watt power supply from Corsair. Not a bad unit. And after the customer got the system back home they turned it on. It worked great for one session and then all of a sudden just died and wouldn't power on. Or at least it would power on, just no display out. Brought it over to my shop and I immediately figured that it was actually an insufficient amount of power despite having the new power supply going to the graphics card. And how I knew this is that there was actually a red LED on the graphics card, which signifies insufficient power on these Asus cards. Confirm this using my Doctor power 3 power supply tester from Thermal Take which showed that the actual 12 volt high power connector was only distributing 150 Watts instead of the rated 450 that this cable is supposed to be able to handle. That big of a difference is definitely Insufficient power, which was causing this GPU to have no display out because it just couldn't turn on all the way. And what ended up causing the low power for this cable? Well I actually happen to do that. They use the wrong cables. And how I was able to actually figure this out were that the cables that they used were actually these flat cables, which Corsair doesn't use on this particular power supply. After looking it up, they're all sleeve. They're supposed to look something like these. Even after changing these cables and connecting the high voltage connector, the system still was getting insufficient power. Did they fry the power supply? Actually no, they actually fried the 12 volt high power connector, which is something I haven't seen quite yet. So this cable actually fried, and if you use it with any power supply, it reads out way under the actual amount of wattage this is supposed to handle. These three connectors should be able to do 150 Watts each, and even hooking it up to a good power supply with the right cables was only getting about 300 Watts, which is definitely too low. So to go and take care of this issue once and for all, I actually installed a dedicated 12 volt high power connector that goes back to two 8 pin connectors on the backside of the power supply, which took care of the issue and allows it to now display out. It definitely Wasn't the most complicated fix, but I definitely thought it deserved a video to go and share with you guys. Yeah, don't use the wrong cables with your power supply. Even if they happen to fit, it doesn't mean they're actually gonna work, and you could definitely damage some of your componentry.

analysis.problem_symptom: System crashes in games, then after a PSU swap by another shop, boots with no display output
analysis.hardware_specs: Asus GPU, 1000W Corsair Power Supply, Thermaltake Doctor Power 3 Tester, 12VHPWR cable
diagnostic_steps: Identify red LED on the Asus GPU indicating insufficient power
Test power distribution using Thermaltake Doctor Power 3 (measured 150W instead of 450W on 12VHPWR)
Inspect cable physical characteristics (flat non-Corsair cables used instead of sleeved)
Test component continuity and connector condition
analysis.root_cause: Incompatible modular cables used during a power supply replacement, causing power starvation and physical damage to the 12VHPWR connector
analysis.solution: Replaced damaged 12VHPWR connector wiring and installed a dedicated native dual-8-pin to 12VHPWR cable from Corsair
analysis.key_tech_takeaway: Even if modular cables physically fit into a power supply from a different series or brand, differing pinouts will destroy components and cause power failure.

title: This Gaming PC Reached 106.9 degrees! #tech #techtok #pcrepair #compu...
transcript: This hot box of a gaming PC is reaching over 106 degrees Celsius on the CPU, causing the system to frequently freeze and has pretty much caused it to become unusable.
